newsitem.title: CHILE: U.S. eco-millionaire charges harassment by Chileans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. eco-millionaire charges harassment by Chileans.

text.p: An American millionaire trying to create a vast nature reserve in southern Chile accused its opponents on Tuesday of bugging his telephone, sending him death threats and swooping over his house in military jets.

Douglas Tompkins, founder of the Esprit clothing chain, said lies had been spread about him in a "harassment campaign" to stop his environmental project, which has been opposed by parts of Chile's military.

His lawyer said military planes and helicopters buzzed Tompkins' house in southern Chile, where he owns some 1,050 square miles (2,700 sq km) of spectacular land that includes glaciers, fjords and some of the last temperate rainforest on the planet.
Some Chilean military officers consider Tompkins' park a security threat because it stretches from the Pacific to the border with Argentina at one of Chile's narrowest points.

"The detractors of this project have begun a new campaign of accusations and harassment ... in which we are charged with all kinds of irregularities and crimes that have never been proved to public opinion, much less in court," Tompkins said at a news conference.

Joined by five leaders of Chile's environmental movement, Tompkins vowed to stick to his stated goal of donating an area of untouched forests the size of Rhode Island to a Chilean environmental foundation and opening it to the public.

"My idea is still to transfer these lands to a Chilean foundation ... and repatriate them, so to speak, to the Chilean people," Tompkins said. The quiet, gray-haired Californian called himself a misunderstood philanthropist.

Tompkins, a major contributor to green groups, made his fortune in the 1980s with the Esprit clothing line but sold most of his stock in the company and began buying huge tracts of virgin forest along the coast of southern Chile.
The project made Chile's government uneasy because the land stretches from the Pacific coast to the Argentine border, prompting officials to accuse him of "cutting Chile in half."

The nature reserve also divided Chileans, meeting fierce hostility from right-wing politicians and business leaders, who think he bankrolls local environmental pressure groups, and from much of the powerful military, who consider it a threat to national security.
Tompkins' supporters called the opposition a smokescreen for well-connected timber and business interests who want to stop Chile's growing environmental movement at all costs.
"We are facing a situation of hostility, with threats even against Tompkins' physical person," Sara Larrain, leader of Chilean environmental group National Ecology Network said.
She said tax authorities were harassing the group by demanding full tax records at 24 hours notice.
Chile's Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza said he doubted there was any official move against Tompkins.

"Every so often Mr. Tompkins decides to pick a fight with the government of Chile for his own reasons," Insulza told reporters. "We are respectful of the law and as long as Mr. Tompkins respects Chilean laws, we won't fight with him."

Accustions in the local media included charges that Tompkins was building secret airstrips on his land, that he had let Israeli soldiers train there and that he was planning to turn the land into a nuclear waste dump.
